summary: A description of NETRJS, a program from the University of Utah for submitting jobs to the remote job service on the UCLA IBM 360/91 across the ARPANET. A user prepares a job file on the Utah TENEX system, and NETRJS sends it and lets the user watch its progress. Utah wrote it because large compute-bound jobs were slowing its own PDP-10.

eli5.summary: Imagine a big homework you send by mail to a faster computer far away. This program does the sending for you and lets you check how far along the work is.

questions: how did utah submit jobs to the ucla 360/91
how does remote job submission work
subtitle: A program for sending compute jobs across the ARPANET to a remote supercomputer.

tldr.problem: The University of Utah's PDP-10 computer was overwhelmed by large, compute-bound jobs that ran for many hours. The UCLA IBM 360/91 was available on the ARPANET for such work, but there was no easy way for Utah users to submit jobs remotely.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJS, written at Utah, lets a user prepare a job file, submit it to the UCLA remote job service via the ARPANET, monitor progress, and retrieve the output when ready. It uses Telnet-like commands adapted for job submission.
tldr.outcome: Utah users could offload expensive compute jobs to UCLA without waiting locally, and UCLA's system could manage remote job submission efficiently. NETRJS became an example of how different sites could cooperate on the early ARPANET.

facts.label: Written at
facts.value: University of Utah, Computer Science Department

today: RFC 325 documents NETRJS, an early example of remote job submission on the ARPANET. It is marked as Unknown status and has not been obsoleted, remaining a historical record of how different network sites cooperated to solve practical computing problems in the earliest days of computer networking.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Since October 1971, the University of Utah's PDP-10 computer running TENEX had been running very large, compute-bound jobs continuously, which degraded interactive response time for other users. UCLA had a high-performance IBM System/360 Model 91 available for batch processing, accessible via the ARPANET. NETRJS was written to allow Utah users to submit jobs to UCLA's Remote Job Service (RJS) system.

The user creates a job file locally, uses NETRJS to send it to UCLA, can monitor the job's progress at UCLA, and when RJS notifies that output is ready, uses NETRJS to retrieve it. This lets Utah users submit long-running jobs without occupying their local computer.
sections.eli5: Utah's computer was slow at math homework, so NETRJS sends the work to UCLA's faster computer across the network, and brings back the answers.

sections.title: How NETRJS Works
sections.content:
NETRJS uses a command interpreter based on Telnet that lets users type commands to interact with the UCLA system. The main commands are SEND.FILE.NAMED (to submit a job file), RETRIEVE.OUTPUT.FROM (to fetch printed or punched output), JOBSTAT (to check job status), and SYSTAT (to see which remote terminals are using RJS).

The program recognizes partially typed commands, like standard Telnet. A user can maintain multiple connections to UCLA for input, output retrieval, and status monitoring. NETRJS uses the control character ^S as an escape to return to its command level, and tabs are set to 8-column stops for compatibility with card-oriented systems.

The escape character is ^S so that remote sites can use NETRJS while also running Telnet sessions without confusion.
sections.eli5: The user types simple commands like 'send' and 'get' to talk to the distant computer, similar to how Telnet works.

sections.title: Design and Data
sections.content:
NETRJS is site-independent and reusable by any TENEX system connected to the ARPANET. It contains no built-in information about valid UCLA terminal IDs; instead, this data comes from a file called PWD.SAV on the Utah system, which is created and updated separately. This lets different sites use NETRJS with their own configuration data.

Job files are converted to card images (80 characters per line, a restriction from the card-oriented IBM OS/360 batch processing). UCLA's RJS software required core allocation for each open connection, so it limited operator connections to manage system load. Output files retrieved via NETRJS can contain up to 255 characters per line, well beyond the card limit.
sections.eli5: The program was designed to work from any computer, with rules learned from files rather than hardcoded, so anyone could use it.

sections.title: A Session Example
sections.content:
A user logs into their local TENEX system, runs NETRJS, which confirms that UCLA's 360/91 is up. The user types commands to send job files (test jobs and test data), then requests that RJS execute them. The RJS system reports that the jobs have been accepted and are being processed.

Later, the user checks the status and sees that printed output is ready. They request RETRIEVE.OUTPUT.FROM PRINTER, and NETRJS transfers the printed results. Similarly, they can retrieve punched card deck output in either object or ASCII format. The user then signs off from RJS and quits NETRJS.
sections.eli5: A user sends code to UCLA, waits a bit, then asks for results, which NETRJS brings back to the local disk.
